entities.name: Baptist Union of Wales
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Baptist Union of Wales (Welsh: Undeb Bedyddwyr Cymru) is one of Wales's most historically significant religious bodies, rooted in the Welsh Baptist tradition that began with the 1649 founding of the first Welsh-language Baptist congregation (Ilston, Gower Peninsula) and developed through the transformative Welsh religious revivals of the 18th and 19th centuries — particularly the 1859 Revival and the 1904-1905 Welsh Revival led by Evan Roberts, one of the most remarkable religious events in modern Christian history.

The 1904-1905 Welsh Revival is one of the most documented and debated events in 20th-century Christian history: within months of beginning, approximately 100,000 people were reported to have converted across Wales (in a country of approximately 1.5 million at the time — roughly 7% of the population). The revival spread internationally, influencing Pentecostalism's emergence (the Azusa Street Revival of 1906 in Los Angeles was influenced by the Welsh Revival), and transformed Welsh social life — reports of decreased alcohol consumption, crime reduction, and the conversion of prominent miners becoming prevalent.

Wales's distinctive Baptist tradition operates primarily in the Welsh language, making the Baptist Union of Wales an important institution for Welsh language preservation and cultural identity. Welsh-language Baptist congregations have been centers of Welsh-language literacy, singing (the Welsh male voice choir tradition emerged partly from Nonconformist chapel culture), and cultural life for over 350 years.
